title: Pedagogical agent
summary:
A pedagogical agent is a concept borrowed from computer science and artificial intelligence and applied to education, usually as part of an intelligent tutoring system (ITS). It is a simulated human-like interface between the learner and the content in an educational environment.

As computer animation progressed, it was adopted by educators to enhance computerized learning. The first versions were more cartoon than person, like Microsoft's Clippy (1997), but with developments in computer animation, pedagogical agents can now look lifelike. By 2006 there was a call to develop modular, reusable agents, and by 2009 a call to enact agent standards.

Distributed cognition theory describes how cognition progresses through collaboration. Pedagogical agents can assist cognitive transfer, operating as artifacts or partners, acting as a cognitive tool equipped with knowledge the user lacks. Socio-cultural learning theory addresses how users develop through interaction with other agents. A pedagogical agent can intervene on request, support tasks the user cannot address, and potentially extend the learner's cognitive reach.

Interaction with pedagogical agents may elicit emotions such as excitement, confusion, frustration, and discouragement, which affect learner motivation. A pedagogical agent can increase cognitive load by distracting learners, but agents can also reduce perceived cognitive load through narration and personalization. As a tutor, a pedagogical agent has not been demonstrated to add benefit in equivalent lessons; however, there is some support for agents increasing learning as presenters of social cues. A co-learner agent is believed to increase self-efficacy. Individualized pedagogical agents can be found across disciplines including medicine, math, law, language learning, automotive, and armed forces.
